Commission Data Show EU Green Bond Issuance Reaches €39 Billion in 2026
- Taxonomy investment: Over €320 billion was invested in EU Taxonomy-aligned activities in 2025.
- Cumulative investment: Over €1.2 trillion has been invested in sustainable activities since 2021.
- Green bond issuance: Around €60 billion has been issued since December 2024.
The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, says over €1.2 trillion has been invested in sustainable activities since 2021. According to the figures, over €320 billion was invested in 2025 in activities aligned with the EU Taxonomy. The Taxonomy is the classification system that helps companies and investors identify environmentally sustainable activities. Meanwhile, the energy sector accounted for the largest share, driven mainly by electricity providers, according to the Commission.
The Commission says the figures also show continued growth in use of the EU’s sustainable finance framework. The framework links economic growth with decarbonisation by supporting the roll-out of clean technologies and infrastructure, especially in the energy sector. By channeling investment into domestic renewable energy, electrification and other clean technologies, the framework reduces reliance on imported fossil fuels, the Commission says. Notably, the release did not describe the methodology used to calculate the investment and issuance figures.
European Green Bonds are also gaining momentum, with around €60 billion issued since December 2024. That total includes €21 billion in 2025 and a further €39 billion from 1 January to 7 October 2026. The Commission says the 2026 amount is nearly double the amount issued in the first year, pointing to growing use of the standard. The European Green Bond Standard is a voluntary framework for bonds that finance Taxonomy-aligned activities.

Who It Affects
- Bond issuers: The European Green Bond Standard is voluntary and applies to bonds that finance Taxonomy-aligned activities.
- Electricity providers: They mainly drove the energy sector’s large share of 2025 Taxonomy-aligned investment, the largest of any sector.
- Companies and investors: The Commission is simplifying the sustainable finance framework to make it easier to implement.

articles.title: ACCC says ads can't present bought carbon credits as emission cuts - PPC Land
articles.summary: ACCC says ads can't present bought carbon credits as emission cuts  PPC Land
articles.full_text:
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission today published guidance telling businesses that marketing which blends purchased carbon credits with real emissions reductions is likely to mislead consumers, setting out one "Golden Rule" and six prompts that will shape how it assesses climate claims in packaging, websites, television and outdoor .
In Short
Australia's consumer watchdog wrote a rulebook for companies that boast in ads about cutting their greenhouse gas emissions. If a company says it cut its pollution in half but really just bought credits from a forest project somewhere else, the watchdog thinks most shoppers would be fooled. From now on, any company making these claims will be judged on what an ordinary person takes away from the ad, not on the fine print or the technical accounting behind it.
What the ACCC published
The document is titled "Making emissions claims to consumers - a guide for business." It runs to 24 numbered pages, carries the reference ACCC 10/26_26-67 and is dated October 2026. The accompanying media release, number 119/26, is dated 20 October 2026.
According to the release, Australian businesses making greenhouse gas emissions claims "should use credible, science-based accounting standards, be transparent about the use of purchased credits, and, above all else, consider what average consumers would understand their claims to mean." The release frames the guide as a tool for businesses that want to promote climate action and need to understand "potentially problematic behaviour and risks in failing to consider the consumer perspective when advertising emissions data."
The legal hook is the Australian Consumer Law, which prohibits false or misleading representations and misleading or deceptive conduct. The ACCC states plainly in the guide that it "is not an environmental regulator." Its role is consumer protection, and the guide reads accordingly: almost every example turns on the gap between what a company's accounts show and what a shopper would believe after seeing a billboard, a swing tag or a social media post.
ACCC Deputy Chair Mick Keogh put the commercial case in two parts. "Consumers should be able to trust the emissions-related claims that businesses make," he said, according to the release. "Greenwashing not only limits the ability of consumers to make informed purchasing decisions, but it also disadvantages businesses that have invested in the development of products or services that are genuinely more environmentally sustainable."
He also acknowledged that the underlying discipline is difficult. "We recognise that greenhouse gas emissions accounting is complex and increasingly regulated. Our guidance is particularly aimed at helping businesses to understand their consumer law obligations when making voluntary marketing claims to consumers," Keogh said. His closing instruction was direct: "If any existing claims raise concerns, businesses should update their messaging, gather stronger evidence, or reconsider using it."
Scope: marketing, not mandatory reporting
The guide covers "product packaging, point of sale promotions, advertising and general website content." It explicitly does not apply to "specifically regulated contexts such as mandatory climate reporting or mandatory labelling." There is a catch, however. Where statements from those regulated contexts are reproduced in consumer-facing claims, according to the ACCC, consumer law applies and businesses are encouraged to consider the guidance.
That carve-back matters for any company that lifts a figure from its sustainability report and drops it into a television spot. Several of the guide's worked examples involve exactly that move, and in each one the ACCC concludes that a technically accurate reported number produced a misleading advertisement.
The guide also builds on, rather than replaces, the ACCC's 2023 publication "Making environmental claims - a guide for businesses," which set out eight principles for trustworthy environmental claims. The new document applies those principles to emissions specifically. On enforcement, it points back to page 34 of the 2023 guide, noting that the regulator will consider whether a business "made genuine efforts and took appropriate steps to verify the accuracy of any information relied on." Smaller businesses get some room: the ACCC says it recognises they "may not have access to the same resources as larger businesses," and that this will be taken into account.
Why publish guidance at all, rather than wait for judgments? The ACCC gives its own answer: "there are limited cases where Australian courts have judged these issues."
The Golden Rule: the dominant message wins
Everything in the guide hangs on what the ACCC calls the Golden Rule: consider the consumer audience, because marketing context matters. The test is the "dominant message, or the overall impression" a claim creates for "an ordinary and reasonable consumer."
Three consequences follow, each with obvious implications for creative and media teams.
First, images count as claims. "Images, colours and icons matter," the guide states. A forest backdrop or a smiling planet can make a business "seem greener than it really is." Two of the worked examples, a hybrid SUV filmed driving through forests and an energy retailer's billboards featuring a smiling Earth, are judged likely to mislead in part because of the imagery.
Second, fine print does not rescue a headline. "Small print, asterisked links, or disclaimers are unlikely to be enough to change the dominant message of a prominent headline claim," according to the guide.
Third, the channel changes what is acceptable. Consumers viewing "a billboard, TV or radio ad may only take in a short, simple message," the guide says, so "complex, technical language and nuanced terms should be avoided." A website, by contrast, "can allow for more detailed explanations." The guide repeatedly suggests moving nuanced material - transition plans, accounting boundaries, credit registries - to web pages or QR codes, while keeping short-form copy to specific, already-achieved facts.
The audience question gets similar treatment. Language suitable for regulators or institutional investors "may be misleading when used in short-form advertisements to a broad cohort of consumers." The ACCC singles out "net zero" as a term that "has a particular meaning in a regulatory or technical context" but may be understood differently by shoppers.
Six prompts, one checklist
Beneath the Golden Rule sit six prompts, summarised in a one-page checklist. Each row poses a question and states what to do if the answer is "no or not sure." The simple rule at the bottom of that table echoes Keogh's quote: "If any check raises concerns, refine your messaging, gather stronger evidence or reconsider using it."
Prompt 1: complete, reputable and clear accounting
Calculations behind a claim must, according to the guide, substantiate the dominant message, show how a figure was reached, use "established, reputable emissions accounting frameworks," compare against realistic baselines "not picked to over or underestimate the true position," include all significant emission sources, explain and justify any omissions, and be understandable "by a person without technical knowledge."
The guide lists five tests for an accounting framework: relevance, completeness, consistency, transparency and accuracy. It also warns that third-party certifications and trust marks do not shift responsibility. Reliance on them "does not change your businesses' responsibility to make sure its claims are not misleading or deceptive."
The worked example is pointed for the digital industry. A social networking business reports a 43% cut in scope 1 and 2 emissions for its Australian arm, driven by renewable energy purchases and a switch from gas to electric heating. It runs a website and television campaign saying "We have reduced our emissions by 43%," with an asterisk referencing its 2025 corporate reporting obligations. The problem is an offshore data centre the company does not own, which is "essential to delivering the social networking services to Australian users." Those emissions would be scope 3, which the company does not yet report. Counting them, the total reduction is 10%.
The ACCC's conclusion: the reasonable consumer "is likely to assume that the business has reduced its overall emissions by 43%," and the asterisk "is not enough to change the dominant message." The suggested compliant version says 10%.
For a sector whose services run on third-party cloud infrastructure, the example is hard to miss. The guide defines scope 3 as emissions "that occur in the value chain of an entity, but which are outside of the business's operational control," citing definitions adapted from ASIC, the Clean Energy Regulator and the Greenhouse Gas Protocol.
Prompt 2: no highly selective or broad claims
The guide names a list of terms that "may create the misleading impression that your business's contribution to combating climate change is more than it currently is" when used in short-form marketing: "clean," "sustainable," "carbon neutral," "climate neutral," "climate positive," "climate friendly," "carbon positive" and "net zero." The risk is highest, according to the ACCC, "when the claim is used to influence consumer purchasing decisions and used in isolation and on product-level marketing."
Words such as "net," "neutral" and "positive" are flagged as ambiguous because consumers may read them as absolute quantities when they are used in a relative sense. Comparisons face the same scrutiny. A phrase like "lower emissions" needs context about what is being compared and why. articles.title: COP17: How Can We End The War on Nature and Biodiversity? - Sustainability Magazine
articles.summary: COP17: How Can We End The War on Nature and Biodiversity?  Sustainability Magazine
articles.full_text:
The UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) takes place in Yerevan, Armenia, from 19 to 30 October 2026, marking a critical halfway point in global efforts to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
The conference plans to assess the progress towards the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), agreed in 2022 and identify where countries must accelerate implementation.
With progress falling short across several targets, governments face growing pressure to turn international commitments into measurable outcomes.
Discussions will aim to focus on conservation, ecosystem restoration, biodiversity finance and the role of businesses in protecting the natural world.
Assesses progress towards global biodiversity targets
The KMGBF provides the international blueprint for addressing biodiversity loss, setting out 23 targets for 2030 and four longer-term goals for 2050.
Its objectives cover the main drivers of nature loss, including land and sea use changes, unsustainable exploitation of species, climate change, pollution and invasive species.
One of its best-known ambitions is the 30-by-30 target, which seeks to conserve 30% of the world's land and sea by 2030.
The framework also addresses biodiversity finance, harmful incentives, sustainable production and consumption and the environmental impacts and dependencies of businesses.
Ahead of COP17, nearly 90% of the 196 parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity had established national biodiversity targets, while close to 60% had developed national biodiversity strategies and action plans.
However, fewer than half of the national targets assessed by participating countries were on track, highlighting the need for faster implementation and stronger accountability.
“Nature is at the heart of our economy and our resilience,” says Jessika Roswall, Commissioner for Environment, Water Resilience and a Competitive Circular Economy.
“The EU is implementing ambitious policies to protect and restore nature and is a major supporter of biodiversity protection worldwide.
“We need to collectively accelerate the implementation of the KMGBF to ensure a future that is sustainable and resilient for all.”
Biodiversity finance remains a critical challenge
Mobilising sufficient funding is a central priority at COP17, as governments seek to close the gap between biodiversity commitments and the resources available to deliver them.
The global framework calls for at least US$200bn annually from all sources by 2030, including at least US$30bn in international biodiversity finance.
The European Union is working to mobilise public and private investment, having committed to doubling its international biodiversity funding from €3.5bn (US$3.9bn) to €7bn (US$7.9bn).
The European Commission has also proposed allocating 35% of the total EU budget and 30% of international financing under the Global Europe instrument to climate and environmental action for the 2028–2034 period.
Nature credits are emerging as a potential mechanism for attracting private investment alongside public funding, although their role in supporting biodiversity outcomes will depend on effective implementation.
“Yerevan should be the COP of proof, not only of promises,” says Teresa Ribera, Executive Vice-President for Clean, Just and Competitive Transition.
“Healthy ecosystems are indispensable for climate resilience, water security, food security and long-term prosperity. Protecting and restoring biodiversity is not a cost.
“It is an investment in our future, our economies and the next generations.
“Now it’s time to turn the ambition of the KMGBF into delivery.”
COP17 also plans to consider arrangements for the Cali Fund, which aims to ensure fair and equitable benefit-sharing from the commercial use of digital sequence information on genetic resources, with proceeds supporting biodiversity conservation and Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
Facing pressure to accelerate implementation
COP17's first global review of collective progress under the KMGBF will aim to examine what has been achieved since 2022 and where further action is required.
Governments will need to address gaps in national implementation, improve monitoring and reporting and strengthen cooperation to measure progress against the framework's 23 targets.
- Dates: October 19–30, 2026.
- Location: Yerevan, Armenia.
- Theme: "Taking Action for Nature".
- Main Focus: The first global review of collective progress under the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), which includes targets to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030 and reform harmful subsidies.
- Symbol: The Anomalous blue butterfly (Polyomatus eriwanensis), an endemic species to Yerevan's grasslands, featuring 23 colours representing the 23 biodiversity targets.
These priorities extend beyond environment ministries, requiring greater integration of biodiversity into finance, business practices, production systems and consumption.
For businesses, the framework highlights the importance of understanding their impacts and dependencies on nature, alongside the need to support more sustainable supply chains and investment decisions.
The EU is also seeking to place Indigenous Peoples and local communities at the centre of nature protection, recognising the importance of their participation in biodiversity governance and conservation.
By bringing these issues together, COP17 offers an opportunity to strengthen accountability and establish clearer pathways from national commitments to measurable results.
Yerevan puts nature protection and economic resilience in focus
The conference comes as biodiversity loss increasingly intersects with concerns over climate resilience, water security, food production and long-term economic prosperity.
Healthy ecosystems underpin the natural resources and services on which communities and businesses depend, making their protection an important part of sustainable development.
Armenia's COP17 presidency has called for the conference to combine a review of global progress with practical measures to accelerate implementation before 2030.
The EU is set to participate in negotiations and promote initiatives intended to mobilise biodiversity finance, strengthen international cooperation and support the delivery of global targets.
Governments will also need to address the persistent shortfalls in funding, capacity and data that continue to limit progress towards the 30-by-30 ambition and wider restoration goals.
With four years remaining until the 2030 deadline, COP17 represents a crucial opportunity to turn the global biodiversity framework into coordinated action that delivers lasting benefits for nature, communities and economies.

articles.title: MEPs back waste exemption for small businesses amid circular economy push - The Brussels Times
articles.summary: MEPs back waste exemption for small businesses amid circular economy push  The Brussels Times
articles.full_text:
Small and micro businesses based in the EU could be temporarily exempted from having to appoint an authorised representative in every member state where they sell products under waste-related rules, after MEPs backed a targeted suspension.
The European Parliament adopted its negotiating position ahead of talks with EU governments on changes affecting producers of packaging, batteries, textiles, footwear, electronics and single-use plastics, the parliamentary press service reported on Tuesday.
Under existing EU rules, producers placing products on the EU market pay fees to help fund the collection, sorting and recycling of those products when they become waste, a system known as extended producer responsibility (EPR).
Companies must also appoint an authorised representative for EPR compliance in each country where they sell.
MEPs supported narrowing a suspension proposed by the European Commission so it would apply only to EU-based small and micro enterprises — defined as firms with fewer than 50 employees and annual turnover or a balance sheet under €10 million — rather than to a broader range of companies.
The exemption would run until 2035, or until a more comprehensive “circular economy act” is adopted.
A circular economy act refers to planned EU-wide rules intended to cover how products and materials are kept in use for longer through measures such as reuse and recycling.
What would and would not change
MEPs said the suspension would not alter other EPR obligations, such as waste-prevention requirements or fees paid under the scheme.
They also called for better information exchange between member states, interoperable digital systems and common reporting requirements for companies operating across the EU single market.
The report’s lead MEP, Ingeborg ter Laak of the centre-right EPP group in the Netherlands, said “unnecessary administrative burdens should be reduced” while companies continued to take responsibility for the waste they produce.
The Parliament’s position on waste batteries and packaging waste passed by 616 votes to 9, with 39 abstentions.
A separate vote covering textiles, footwear, electronic appliances and single-use plastics passed by 612 votes to 8, with 39 abstentions.
Negotiations on the final laws can begin once the Council of the EU — representing EU member states — has also agreed its position.

articles.title: Sovereigns set to be relegated to technical negotiations in SFDR trilogue - Responsible Investor
articles.summary: Sovereigns set to be relegated to technical negotiations in SFDR trilogue  Responsible Investor
articles.full_text:
The question of general purpose sovereign bonds is set to be relegated to a technical negotiation in the EU’s first trilogue meeting on the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) this Thursday.
The meeting will set out issues for both political and technical negotiation, with safeguards on fossil fuel investments for the Transition category expected to be a point of contention.
Under the trilogue, negotiators for the European Parliament and Council of the EU will seek to reconcile their differences of opinion on various issues.
These are split into two “tiers” – political and technical negotiations – which run separately.
Political issues cover key areas of divergence which are particularly contentious, whereas technical matters are those with less political risk or for which the negotiating positions are closely aligned.
However, if negotiators fail to agree on technical issues, they can be elevated to political status in order to receive guidance from high-level negotiators.
Member states were asked to approve the treatment of general purpose sovereign bonds being relegated to a technical discussion at a meeting on Monday last week, according to a working paper seen by Responsible Investor.
The sovereign question has been a key issue for investors watching negotiations. Both Council and Parliament have aligned on allowing limited amounts of general purpose EU public sector debt into Transition funds, albeit with some technical differences.
Leonie Timmers, of counsel at HSF Kramer, said sovereign debt had been an “intense Council-internal political fight”, as member states negotiated on rules that will affect demand for their own debt.
However, she said it was “settled with a specific, negotiated figure everyone could live with”, while Parliament landed on a similar proposal.
“The fight had effectively already happened, and what’s left is implementation detail, which is why I believe the presidency proposes moving it to the technical track.”
An opt-out regime for alternative funds, precise wording of human rights exclusions, implementation timelines, engagement strategy, and disclosure and naming rules for non-categorised products will all also be delegated to the technical level.
Political problems
The key political issue is expected to be exclusions for Transition funds.
Member states have backed an exclusion of fossil fuel companies unless they have a Paris-aligned emissions reduction target and spend 20 percent of capex on taxonomy-aligned activities.
Parliament’s position requires the taxonomy capex spend to also be higher than capex on new fossil fuel projects, and for companies to have a time-bound plan to phase out coal mining for power generation.
Timmers said she expected fossil fuel exclusions to be the “sharpest fight” in trilogue, after significant internal debate among member states on their eventual decision.
Parliament’s own position “widens the gap that co-legislators now have to close”, she added.
RI reported last week that delegates from France, Portugal, Spain, Germany and Poland also criticised the Parliament stance at a meeting of Council representatives on Monday, where the issue was the top item on the agenda.
According to the working paper, other issues slated for political discussions include how to deal with temporary breaches of category exclusions criteria, which principal adverse impact indicators funds should be required to disclose against and entity-level disclosures.
There are several differences between Parliament and Council on these issues, especially on PAI indicators, for which the latter is proposing a more flexible and permissive regime compared with prescribed indicators set by Parliament.
Timmers said this showed a “real disagreement about purpose: flexibility and product-tailored disclosure versus comparability and supervisory consistency”.
The file is expected to be finalised by the end of the year, which would require negotiations to conclude before the start of December.
Following a provisional agreement, the resulting text will need to be reviewed and signed off by a body of EU member state ambassadors, known as Coreper. Only one meeting of Coreper’s Economic and Financial Affairs Council is scheduled for the month – on 11 December.
The text will then return to Parliament and EU member states for final vetting and approval.

articles.title: Publication of forest boundary maps: A database to support businesses in meeting EUDR regulations. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Publication of forest boundary maps: A database to support businesses in meeting EUDR regulations.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On October 20th, the Department of Forestry and Forest Protection ( Ministry of Agriculture and Environment ) held a technical meeting to announce the 2020 Forest Boundary Map version 1.0 (VFM2020.v1). This is an important step towards building a unified spatial data system nationwide, creating a legal and technical basis to support key export sectors such as timber, coffee, and rubber in demonstrating that their products are not related to deforestation or forest degradation according to the European Union's Regulation on Deforestation Prevention and Control (EUDR).
Publication of forest boundary maps: A database to support businesses in meeting EUDR regulations.
(Chinhphu.vn) - The EUDR regulations impose very strict requirements on legality, geographic traceability down to the production plot, and evidence proving that the product does not cause deforestation or forest degradation after December 31, 2020. For Vietnam, sectors with large export turnover to the EU, such as agricultural and forestry products (wood, coffee, rubber), are directly affected by these regulations.
Speaking at the meeting, Mr. Nguyen Van Dien, Deputy Director of the Department of Forestry and Forest Protection, emphasized that meeting EUDR standards is both a major challenge and an opportunity for Vietnam's forestry sector to innovate management methods, accelerate the digital transformation of forest resource data, and enhance the brand reputation of its products in the international market.
The VFM2020.v1 map was developed to provide a unified source of spatial data at the national level. Through this map, state management agencies, local authorities, and the business community can easily look up and check the overlap between agricultural and forestry production areas and the current forest boundaries as of 2020. Notably, the map helps accurately identify areas planted with coffee or rubber trees that provide shade, classified as non-forested land, minimizing the risk of confusion with deforestation activities. All this data has been publicly integrated on the WebGIS platform at: eudr.vnforest.gov.vn.
According to Dr. Pham Van Duan, Deputy Director of the Institute of Forest Ecology and Environment, VFM2020.v1 integrates forest monitoring data provided by localities, combined with remote sensing image processing, international reference map sources, and field survey results. Local data serves as the core input platform, while satellite imagery and international data are applied to detect and compare discrepancies.
The map creation process was carried out rigorously through six technical steps: Standardizing the 2020 forest status data; Reviewing the planning maps for the three types of forests; Assessing reliability from multiple data sources; Analyzing forest area changes using remote sensing technology; Reviewing, verifying, and agreeing on results with local authorities; Completing and integrating the database into the WebGIS system.
The map classifies data into three reliability levels: High reliability: When all data sources are completely consistent; Medium reliability: When there are small discrepancies between sources; Areas requiring review: When significant differences appear between domestic forest status maps, international reference data, and remote sensing imagery. These locations are forwarded to local authorities for comparison with management records and field verification.
According to a report by Mr. Pham Ngoc Hai (Forest Survey and Planning Institute - FIPI, Vietnam Academy of Forestry Science), within the area of forest land with available data, the overall agreement rate between the two maps reached 78.5%, with a difference rate of 21.5%. Notably, for natural forest areas, the overlap rate reached 92%.
Geographically, the highest level of agreement between the two maps was in the Central Highlands (80.3%), followed by the North (77.6%) and the South (65.7%). This necessitates a review process that is specific to each ecological region and actual land use characteristics.
The head of the Forestry and Forest Protection Department noted that the VFM2020.v1 map is a base data source for inspection, lookup, and comparison, and is not the sole legal basis for concluding whether a shipment meets EUDR regulations. To complete the compliance assessment dossier, businesses are required to provide complete traceability documents, geographical coordinates of the growing area, and relevant field evidence as required by the EU.
Version 1.0 is defined as the initial step in building an open database, not a fixed, closed product. In the future, the Department of Forestry and Forest Protection will continue to coordinate with research institutes, local authorities, industry associations, and the business community to review and update data changes and issue unified technical guidelines.
Exporting businesses are advised to proactively utilize the WebGIS system and promptly report any discrepancies (including precise coordinates and verification documents) so that relevant agencies can coordinate and address them.

articles.title: SFDR 2.0: The overhaul takes shape - A&O Shearman
articles.summary: SFDR 2.0: The overhaul takes shape  A&O Shearman
articles.full_text:
The Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) is undergoing a fundamental transformation. Almost a year after the European Commission published its long-awaited legislative proposal on November 20, 2025, the co-legislative process is now well advanced. The European Parliament (EP) and the Council of the EU have adopted their respective positions, and trilogue negotiations are expected to open on October 22, 2026 under the Irish Presidency, with both co-legislators aiming for a deal before the end of that Presidency, although the final agreement could slip into early 2027.
Application is not expected before January 1, 2029, as both co-legislators provide for application 24 months after entry into force.
This alert provides EEA and non-EEA asset managers with a clear-eyed assessment of where the discussions stand today and where the points of contention lie.
The direction of travel is unambiguous: SFDR 2.0 will replace what was originally a disclosure-only framework with a prescriptive product categorisation regime, backed by binding investment thresholds, mandatory exclusions, and strict naming and marketing rules. The strategic question for every asset manager is no longer whether to engage with the new framework, but how and when.
For our initial analysis of the Commission proposal, see our eAlert: SFDR 2.0: overhaul impact of the new categories and disclosures on funds and asset managers.
From disclosure to categorisation
The Commission’s proposal marks a decisive pivot. Under the current SFDR, Articles 8 and 9 are designed as disclosure obligations, not product labels. In practice, however, the market treated them as quasi-labels, creating inconsistent market practices, supervisory friction, and greenwashing risk.
The Commission’s proposal replaces this ambiguity with three explicit, criteria-based product categories:
- Transition (Article 7): For products investing in, or contributing to, clear and measurable transition objectives relating to sustainability factors. This fills a longstanding policy gap by formally recognising transition finance strategies, including engagement-based approaches, provided they are combined with another credible transition route and credible decarbonisation plans.
- ESG Basics (Article 8): For products with credible ESG integration that goes beyond the mere consideration of sustainability risks. This is the broadest category, designed for a range of ESG approaches.
- Sustainable (Article 9): For products pursuing clear and measurable sustainability objectives, such as investments in companies or assets that already meet high sustainability standards.
Categorisation is mandatory for any product wishing to make sustainability-related claims in its name or marketing communications.
Alongside these three standalone categories, a new Article 9a addresses financial products that combine categorised products or otherwise mix investment approaches, such as funds-of-funds, multi-option products, and pension or insurance-based investment products offering a choice of underlying options.
This combined product category can be further sub-divided into:
- Categorised combined products that meet the 70% threshold of a single category (Article 9a (1)): for products that meet (i) the 70% threshold of a single category by combining investments in categorised products and/or eligible investments of the relevant category and (ii) the applicable exclusions. These products are treated as falling within that category.
- Non-categorised combined products that do not meet the 70% threshold of a single category (Article 9a (2)): for products investing in at least two categorised products but falling short of the threshold for a single category. They are treated as non-categorised products but may disclose the share of underlying categorised products and their composition through the pre-contractual disclosures of underlying categorised products. Direct holdings of eligible investments do not count towards the threshold.
Impact add-on for transition and sustainable categories
Impact investing is formally recognised and protected by an “impact add-on” available for Transition and Sustainable products that have the objective of generating pre-defined, positive and measurable social or environmental impact. Only products using the add-on may use “impact” in their names.
Common architecture to the three proposed categories
All three categories share a common structural framework:
- A binding 70% minimum investment threshold linked to the category’s stated objective, measured using credible sustainability indicators. A phase-in period is permitted, recognising that alternative and private asset strategies require time to deploy capital fully.
- Safe harbours for Transition and Sustainable categories: Portfolios tracking or managed by reference to an EU Climate Transition Benchmark (CTB) or Paris-Aligned Benchmark (PAB) are deemed to meet the criteria of the relevant category. A minimum 15% EU Taxonomy-aligned investments threshold also creates an EU Taxonomy safe harbour for the 70% criterion.
- Eligible investment types: a non-exhaustive list accommodating diverse approaches, including best-in-class (against a benchmark or proven track record), transition strategies with transition plan or science-based targets, and investments in EU Green Bonds or EuSEFs. Engagement strategies are not a standalone-eligible ESG strategy and must be combined with another transition route.
- Minimum exclusions: the applicable exclusions become progressively stricter across the categories.
| Exclusions | ART 7 | ART 8 | ART 9 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| CTB exclusions (controversial weapons, tobacco, UNGC principles and OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises (OECD Guidelines)) | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| PAB exclusions: companies deriving: |  |  |  | 
|  | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
|  | No | No | Yes | 
| New fossil fuel exclusions: |  |  |  | 
|  | Yes | No | Yes | 
Transition and Sustainable categories benefit from exceptions from the prohibited investments above.
| Exceptions to excluded investments | ART 7 | ART 8 | 
|---|---|---|
| Use of proceeds of: |  |  | 
|  | Yes | Yes | 
|  | No | Yes | 
| Provided that the issuer: |  |  | 
|  | Yes | Yes | 
|  | No | Yes | 
- Principal Adverse Impacts (PAIs) disclosures for Transition and Sustainable categories: Transition and Sustainable products must identify and disclose principal adverse impacts and actions taken to address PAIs.
Non-categorised products (Article 6A)
Products that do not meet the criteria for any category face tight restrictions. Under a new Article 6a, non-categorised products may include limited, neutral information on sustainability factors in pre-contractual disclosures, but this information must not be a “central element” (i.e., occupy less than 10% of the investment strategy section in volume) and must not constitute a sustainability-related claim. Non-categorised products cannot use ESG-related terms in their names or sustainability-related claims in marketing communications.
Key simplifications and reduced scope
The proposed revised framework eliminates several burdensome features of the current regime:
- Financial advisers and credit institutions or investment firms providing portfolio management are carved out from SFDR scope.
- Entity-level PAI statements and remuneration policy disclosures are deleted.
- EU Taxonomy disclaimer is removed.
- Article 10 product website disclosures are no longer required as a standalone document. Pre-contractual and periodic disclosures must still be made available on the FMP’s website, although hyperlinks will suffice.
- Pre-contractual disclosure templates are capped at two pages (three pages for impact products).
- The definition of “sustainable investment” (including the Do-No-Significant-Harm test) is removed, with the underlying concepts embedded within the product categories and operationalised through minimum exclusions.
- While an earlier draft permitted an opt-out for AIFs marketed exclusively to professional investors, this was removed from the final Commission text.
That proposal is not the final law: it is the starting point for negotiations between the Council of the EU, representing the Member States’ governments and the EP, representing EU citizens, and its content may still change significantly. The two co-legislators, the EP and the Council, each examine the Commission’s proposal separately and adopt their own position, often amending the Commission’s text. Both co-legislators have now settled their positions, so the three institutions can meet in informal negotiations known as “trilogues”, with the Commission acting as a facilitator, to agree a single compromise text. The following section describes where each legislator stands before the trilogues start.
Where things stand
The period since November 2025 has been marked by intensive institutional activity. The ordinary legislative procedure is now actively progressing along two parallel institutional tracks:
- Council of the EU: On June 24, 2026, the Council agreed its negotiating mandate on SFDR 2.0. The category names remain provisional. The Council text is, broadly, more industry-friendly than the EP position on the issues of greatest operational significance.
- EP: The ECON Committee adopted its negotiating position on September 10, 2026, which was officially endorsed by the EP on October 7, 2026.
- Trilogue: Interinstitutional negotiations are expected to commence in October 2026. A political agreement on the Level 1 text could be reached by the end of 2026 or in early 2027.
The three institutions agree on the fundamental architecture:
- three product categories
- the 70% investment threshold concept
- the disclosure of PAIs
- the concept of an EU Taxonomy safe harbour (but with diverging thresholds)
- the CTB/PAB safe harbour for Transition and Sustainable products (although the EP has considered its deletion)
- the removal of financial adviser

articles.title: COP 17: Countries on course to miss most global biodiversity targets agreed in 2022 - National Herald
articles.summary: COP 17: Countries on course to miss most global biodiversity targets agreed in 2022  National Herald
articles.full_text:
Governments around the world are on course to miss most of the global biodiversity targets agreed at a United Nations summit in Montreal in 2022, raising concerns about the pace of efforts to protect nature and reverse ecosystem decline.
The agreement, adopted at the COP15 biodiversity summit, committed countries to protecting 30 per cent of the planet, restoring nearly a third of degraded ecosystems and reforming at least $500 billion in environmentally harmful subsidies. However, a report assessing progress towards these goals indicates that countries are falling significantly short of their commitments.
The United Kingdom, which had called for ambitious action during the Montreal negotiations, is on track to meet only three of the agreement's 23 targets by the end of the decade. Countries are gathering at COP17 in Yerevan, Armenia, to review progress and discuss the next steps.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned ahead of the summit that the lack of progress meant “the war on nature has not ended” and that “nature will not survive on good intentions”.
He also called for governments to end subsidies for fossil fuels, arguing that they were contributing to climate change and biodiversity loss.
“Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide,” Guterres said, urging governments to redirect the money towards people and the planet.
“There’s a massive gap between countries agreeing to do something and actually doing it,” said Zac Goldsmith, a former UK government minister who was involved in the period when the agreement was reached.
British conservationists have criticised the gap between the government's international commitments and its domestic policies.
The UK government has weakened biodiversity net-gain rules in England, reduced funding for rainforest protection as part of aid cuts and rejected an outright ban on bottom trawling in marine protected areas, according to conservation campaigners. Natural England has also designated no new sites of special scientific interest to protect rare wildlife and habitats since 2023.
Craig Bennett, head of The Wildlife Trusts, said the UK needed to demonstrate that it could deliver on its commitments at home before urging other countries to meet their targets.
“For us to go around the world telling other countries that they must achieve these targets without us having a plan how to deliver them at home is a form of neocolonialism,” he said.
A UK government spokesperson said the government had backed nature recovery and climate resilience with £7 billion in funding and introduced powers to tackle water pollution, support species recovery and fund international conservation.
The government has also reinstated international climate finance commitments, pledging around £6 billion from its aid budget over the next three financial years, with approximately a quarter expected to be spent on nature.
Jonathan Hall, managing director of Conservation International UK, welcomed the renewed commitment but called for greater transparency over how the funding would be spent.
Efforts to protect biodiversity have faced political opposition in several countries, particularly where environmental measures affect agriculture and other economic interests.
In the Netherlands, EU measures introduced to tackle nitrogen pollution and protect vulnerable ecosystems triggered widespread farmer protests. The EU's nature restoration law, part of its wider environmental policy framework, also faced opposition from right-wing lawmakers in the European Parliament before being passed in a substantially weakened form.
Steven Guilbeault, Canada's former environment minister who helped guide the 2022 negotiations alongside China's environment minister Huang Runqiu, said governments often struggled to explain complex environmental policies to the public.
The return of Donald Trump to the US presidency has also dealt a blow to conservation funding, with cuts to the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and other government agencies leaving numerous projects without financial support.
Several European countries have also reduced funding despite committing to increase biodiversity finance to $30 billion annually by the end of the decade. The UK has restricted access to the Darwin Initiative, excluding at least 89 countries from eligibility earlier this year.
Attempts to mobilise private-sector funding have also fallen short. A fund intended to support companies using digital biodiversity data for commercial discoveries has reportedly raised only $6,000, despite hopes that it would generate hundreds of millions of dollars annually.
Despite the setbacks, some countries have made progress towards the biodiversity agreement's goals. One estimate suggests that countries could come close to meeting the target of protecting 30% of land, while the agreement has also helped formalise Indigenous territories in several countries.
French Polynesia has established large marine parks, while Kazakhstan has pursued rewilding initiatives, including efforts to reintroduce the Caspian tiger.
However, conservationists say these gains remain insufficient to address the scale of the crisis.
Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said promised national plans and committed funding were failing to materialise at the required pace.
“Protection targets are falling short, promised national plans have yet to materialise, and committed finance is not reaching where it is needed,” he said.
With countries meeting in Armenia to review progress, the central challenge remains translating international commitments into effective domestic policies, sustained funding and measurable improvements in biodiversity.

articles.title: Biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning underpins the achievement of global biodiversity targets - Nature
articles.summary: Biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning underpins the achievement of global biodiversity targets  Nature
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Target 1 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM-GBF) mandates Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (hereafter, Parties) to address biodiversity loss across all regions within their national jurisdictions by 2030 in part by implementing participatory, integrated and biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning (BISP).
In this Perspective, we outline how delivering Target 1 is foundational to many other KM-GBF targets, directing restoration (Target 2), optimizing protected and conserved area networks (Target 3), and actions to prevent extinctions (Target 4).
Biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning will also support addressing biodiversity threats (Targets 6–8) and guide sustainable use across production systems and urban landscapes (Targets 5, 9–12).
Participatory and inclusive spatial planning will also advance equity objectives such as fair benefit-sharing and the recognition of Indigenous peoples and local communities, and influencing all levels of decision-making (Targets 14, 21–23).
The central challenge to delivering Target 1 is to move beyond siloed approaches; Parties should integrate planning into unified spatial planning frameworks that improve coherence, maximize benefits, minimize threats and reduce trade-offs.
The ambitions of the KM-GBF will only be achieved if Parties give priority to Target 1 and align existing planning elements, tools and approaches into coherent spatial strategies capable of systemically halting and reversing biodiversity loss.

Key points
- Target 1 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM-GBF) requires all areas within national jurisdictions to be brought under participatory, integrated and biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning (BISP) by 2030.
- Spatial planning is not a new discipline, but BISP is an approach that makes existing spatial planning more biodiversity-inclusive by planning to help to halt and reverse biodiversity loss within statutory, rights-based planning across entire jurisdictions.
- Delivering and implementing Target 1 underpins many KM-GBF targets, including those covering progress on restoration, protected areas, species recovery, threat reduction, sustainable use and mainstreaming targets across the KM-GBF.
- The principal barrier to BISP is often not a lack of technical tools but insufficient integration across realms and sectors, financing, political will and governance capacity to apply them consistently; biodiversity data gaps also exist, especially for aquatic ecosystems.
- Genuine trade-offs between biodiversity, production and development are inevitable and cannot always be reconciled, and effective planning must make these choices and trade-offs explicit rather than assume that they can be eliminated.
- Respecting the rights of Indigenous peoples and local communities, including free, prior and informed consent, is an obligation, not merely a means to more durable conservation outcomes.
- Countries should give priority to establishing the BISP framework itself, building on existing good practice, even where full implementation cannot be completed by 2030.

A major milestone in Cabka’s decarbonization journey
Amsterdam, Netherlands - 19 October 2026 - Cabka N.V. (together with its subsidiaries “Cabka”, or the “Company”), a company specialized in transforming hard to recycle plastic waste into innovative Reusable Transport Packaging (RTP), listed at Euronext Amsterdam, today announces that its near-term science-based emissions reduction targets have been validated by SBTi Services, the validation body of the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi). This important milestone provides a clear and measurable pathway for reducing emissions across our operations and value chain.
The validation builds on Cabka’s existing progress in reducing the carbon footprint of our operations and products, while continuing to expand the circular economy. Cabka committed to the set near-term science-based emissions reduction targets in 2024, aiming to achieve validation in 2026. This milestone has now been achieved on schedule.
“SBTi validation is an important milestone for Cabka,” said Alexander Masharov, CEO of Cabka. “Our priority is to deliver measurable emissions reductions through renewable electricity, more efficient operations and keeping more plastics in the loop. Expanding BuyBack and increasing the use of recycled materials will be central to turning our climate commitments into results.”
Validated targets
Cabka has set a target to reduce absolute scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by 79.79% by 2030 from a 2022 base year. We have also set a target to reduce absolute scope 3 GHG emissions from purchased goods and services and the end-of-life treatment of sold products by 35.0% by 2036 from a 2022 base year.
Measurable progress
From 2022 to 2025, Cabka’s market-based scope 1 and 2 emissions decreased by approximately 66%, driven by the switch to renewable electricity across our sites. That is more than four fifths of the distance to the validated 2030 target. Over the same period, total reported scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, including exclusions, fell by approximately 15%.
Scope 3 remains the largest share of Cabka’s footprint. Reducing it, through raw material choices and the end-of-life treatment of sold products, is the focus of the 2036 target.
Ambition beyond the validated targets
The validated targets define our science-based pathway. On this basis, we continue to pursue our broader company ambition of 100% renewable energy and carbon-neutral own operations by 2030. That ambition goes beyond the validated targets and continues to guide our investment choices.
We will keep reducing emissions across our operations and value chain, with circularity, renewable electricity, energy efficiency and material choices at the heart of our approach.

articles.title: Google and McKinsey Contract 320,000 Tonnes of Carbon Removal From Working Trees
articles.summary:
Symbiosis Coalition has announced long-term offtake agreements to buy carbon removal from Working Trees. Symbiosis members Google and McKinsey have collectively contracted 320,000 tonnes over 10 years. This is also […]
The post Google and McKinsey Contract 320,000 Tonnes of Carbon Removal From Working Trees appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Google and McKinsey Contract 320,000 Tonnes of Carbon Removal From Working Trees
- Offtake volume: Google and McKinsey have collectively contracted 320,000 tonnes over 10 years.
- Project scale: 8,700 hectares restored within a 50,000 hectare project in the Amazon and Cerrado.
- Native species goal: The native share rises from a minimum of 25 per cent to 50 per cent by 2030.
Symbiosis Coalition has announced long-term offtake agreements to buy carbon removal from Working Trees. Symbiosis members Google and McKinsey have collectively contracted 320,000 tonnes over 10 years. This is also Symbiosis Coalition’s first silvopasture project.
According to the release, Working Trees converts primarily degraded cattle pastures into mixed-species silvopasture. Additionally, the project plants rows of commercial timber and native trees into existing pasture for cattle to graze. Notably, commercial species such as African Mahogany and Teak grow on a predictable schedule, which makes their carbon easier to estimate. “
Using a mix of native and non-native tree species can be the right approach for designing projects that are both durable and ecologically positive. Fast-growing non-native species can provide early biomass accumulation and economic returns, while native species contribute long-lived, dense-wood carbon stocks that enhance the permanence of climate benefits. A diversified species mix also enables multiple harvest cycles and a broader range of products, including non-timber forest products. Notably, native trees help projects move beyond a ‘carbon-only’ objective by supporting local biodiversity, habitat quality, and wider ecosystem resilience,” said Daniel Piotto, Associate Professor of Dendrology at the Federal University of Southern Bahia, Brazil, and Symbiosis Coalition Technical Advisory Board Member.
The 8,700 hectares restored sit within a 50,000 hectare project across the southeastern Amazon and central Cerrado. Also, the native species target rises from a minimum of 25 per cent to 50 per cent by 2030, working with Brazilian research institutes. Neither announcement discloses the price or start date, and a separate announcement put the removal at 270,000 tons instead of 320,000 tonnes.
“Silvopasture is one of the most underused tools we have for nature-based carbon removal, and what excites us about the Working Trees project is how much room there is to scale it. Working Trees’ project is sequestering carbon while also improving the land that communities rely on. That’s the kind of outcome we strive for at Symbiosis, real climate impact that supports the livelihoods of the communities this project touches while thinking holistically about landscape-level impacts that last,” said Julia Strong, Executive Director of Symbiosis Coalition.
Track Record
Working Trees piloted the approach across more than 2,000 hectares before this project. Additionally, a separate announcement says a digital platform lets ranchers track every tree planted.
“Our mission at Working Trees is to mobilize the next generation of cattle ranching – where producers and nature thrive together – by partnering with ranchers to deploy silvopasture at the million-hectare scale. However, landscape-level change is not built on one-off transactions. It takes long-term partners on both sides – ranchers who commit to decades of restoration activities and buyers who commit to funding that behavior change. The Symbiosis Coalition is that kind of critical long-term partner, and we’re proud to build alongside them to improve livelihoods, regenerate pasturelands, and mitigate climate change,” said Leif Gonzales-Kramer, CEO of Working Trees.
“Scaling high-integrity nature-based carbon removal is an essential part of our sustainability strategy. By supporting Working Trees’ silvopasture model, we are backing a replicable approach to sustainable land use, unlocking large carbon sinks while strengthening the resilience of local economies,” said Isabelle Schuhmann, Global Director of Environmental Sustainability, McKinsey & Company.

Why It Matters
For Google and McKinsey, the offtakes secure 320,000 tonnes of removal over 10 years from a silvopasture project. For Working Trees, the offtakes add contracted buyers for a project across the Amazon and Cerrado, where ranchers also earn timber revenue. If buyer commitments continue, Working Trees could extend silvopasture toward its million-hectare scale goal.

articles.full_text:
$50 Million From AIIB Backs TPG Global South Climate Fund
- Commitment size: AIIB has committed USD50 million to the fund.
- Co-investment room: AIIB will also provide up to USD50 million in co-investments.
- Regional focus: The fund supports climate investment across AIIB members in Asia, the Middle East and Africa.
The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) has committed USD50 million to the TPG Rise Climate Global South Initiative Fund. AIIB will also provide up to USD50 million in co-investments, bringing its potential total to USD100 million. The fund is a parallel vehicle to TPG Rise Climate II, run in partnership with ALTÉRRA.
It is designed to attract long-term private capital for high-impact climate opportunities in emerging and developing economies. Separately, the release describes ALTÉRRA as one of the largest climate investment platforms in the world. The fund targets energy transition, green mobility, sustainable fuels, sustainable materials and products, carbon solutions, and climate adaptation and resilience.
“Mobilizing private capital is one of AIIB’s core thematic priorities and fundamental to closing the climate investment gap in emerging markets,” said Kim-See Lim, AIIB Chief Investment Officer, Public Sector (Region 1) & Financial Institutions and Funds (Global) Clients. “Through this partnership with TPG, AIIB is supporting the expansion of innovative climate solutions in emerging markets, while strengthening climate finance ecosystems across our members, in line with our corporate target to direct 50% of annual financing to private-sector-oriented operations by 2030.”
The fund is classified as Article 9 under the EU Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation, which covers products with sustainable investment as an objective. AIIB’s participation should also help catalyze additional private capital alongside TPG Rise Climate and other co-investors. It also supports commitments under the Paris Agreement and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. The release did not disclose a target fund size, final close date or co-investor names.
Why It Matters
For AIIB, the commitment advances its goal of directing 50% of annual financing to private-sector-oriented operations by 2030. For TPG, the vehicle adds a Global South parallel fund alongside TPG Rise Climate II. If co-investments follow, the vehicle could give TPG a route to climate projects across AIIB members.

articles.full_text:
1,797 MW Geothermal Base Gives Türkiye a COP31 Platform, IGA Says
- Installed capacity: 1,797 MW at the end of 2025, fourth globally and first in Europe.
- Growth record: No other country has grown its geothermal capacity over 15 years as Türkiye has.
- Net-zero role: Geothermal sits in Türkiye’s path to its 2053 net-zero target.
Türkiye can showcase its geothermal experience as host of COP31, the UN climate conference, says Marit Brommer. Brommer is chief executive of the International Geothermal Association (IGA). Türkiye ranks fourth globally and first in Europe, with 1,797 MW of installed geothermal capacity at the end of 2025. However, the interview gives no geothermal capacity target or investment figure.
Brommer also cites district heating, agriculture and local economic development as areas where Türkiye could lead by example. Notably, Brommer says no other country has grown its geothermal capacity over a 15-year period as Türkiye has. Türkiye’s experience in resource development, investment, regulation and direct use offers lessons for emerging markets in Central Asia, the Balkans and Africa.
“We should look beyond geothermal solely as an electricity technology,” said Marit Brommer, chief executive of the International Geothermal Association.
RELATED ARTICLE: EU COP31 Climate Deal to Accelerate Emissions Cuts
Speaking at the 25th World Petroleum Council (WPC) Energy Congress in Riyadh, Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar placed geothermal in the net-zero path. He said Türkiye is assessing all renewable options, including geothermal, to meet rising demand and reach its 2053 net-zero target. Additionally, he cited AI data centres, electric transport and cooling as drivers of higher electricity consumption. “Through COP31, we aim to send a strong message to the global community on electrification, energy security, and the fight against climate change,” he said.
Who It Affects
- Governments: Clarify resource rights, set transparent licensing procedures, create exploration risk mitigation mechanisms and provide stable long-term investment conditions.
- Investors: High upfront costs, decades-long returns, exploration risk and long permitting procedures can deter investment, even where the geology is good.
- Regulators and financial institutions: Need the capacity to support geothermal projects, alongside public authorities.

articles.full_text:
Amazon Backs Feasibility Work on 960 MW Indiana Nuclear Project
- Project scope: A 12-unit Xe-100 plant with 960 MW of proposed capacity.
- Amazon funding: Amazon provides certain project development funding for the feasibility work.
- Collaboration goal: Second commercial deployment toward more than 5 GW of new U.S. nuclear capacity by 2039.
X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) have announced a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) to advance feasibility work. The work covers a proposed 960 MW Xe-100 small modular reactor (SMR) project in Indiana. Amazon is providing certain project development funding for the effort. The project would also be the second commercial deployment under the collaboration between Amazon and X-energy.
The 12-unit plant would redevelop an AEP-owned brownfield (previously developed) site near the former Breed Generating Station in Sullivan County, Indiana. Together, the proposed project would combine AEP’s power generation and nuclear operating expertise, Amazon’s milestone-based development capital and X-energy’s advanced nuclear technology. The companies did not disclose the project’s cost, construction timeline or power purchaser.
“Advanced nuclear energy has the potential to provide dependable power for over half a century while supporting economic growth in our communities. With this development plan, we are working to bring together the resources to help meet unprecedented growth in energy demand with reliable baseload power while protecting affordability for existing customers. Our agreements with Amazon and X-energy will provide all necessary capital protections and financial safeguards that we have said are essential for any potential nuclear project to move forward,” said Bill Fehrman, Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer of AEP.
The Xe-100 is an 80 MWe (megawatts electric) high-temperature, gas-cooled reactor that uses helium coolant and tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) fuel. The U.S. Department of Energy calls this fuel the “most robust nuclear fuel on earth” because it withstands extreme temperatures without melting. Meanwhile, since 2025, Governor Mike Braun and the Indiana General Assembly have enacted supportive state policies, including investment and manufacturing tax credits.
“Indiana is building an energy future that prioritizes affordability for Hoosier families and businesses while driving economic growth. The decision by I&M/AEP, Amazon and X-energy to explore this technology in one of Indiana’s counties represents the kind of innovation and investment that can deliver lasting benefits for our state. This project has the potential to create well-paying jobs in Sullivan County, strengthen our electric grid and further position Indiana as a national leader in advanced nuclear energy,” said Indiana Governor Mike Braun.
Track Record
The project is intended to be the second grid-scale partnership in the collaboration. It is also the third announced commercial U.S. Xe-100 project, within an approximate 11.5 GW commercial pipeline. “At Amazon, we are committed to serving the needs of our customers and achieving our Climate Pledge goal to be net-zero carbon across our operations by 2040. This collaboration with AEP and X-energy would enable us to make progress on both while ensuring that Indiana’s communities benefit. Together, we’re looking to develop nearly a gigawatt of carbon-free power for the regional grid and pay our full costs without passing them to others. This project would also create jobs and generate tax revenues to benefit Hoosier communities for decades to come,” said Josh Weissman, VP of Data Center Infrastructure Capacity Delivery at Amazon. “This partnership brings together the experience, ambition, and innovation needed to move a project of this significance forward. AEP’s 50years of excellence in nuclear operations, combined with the world-class expertise of Amazon and technology of X-energy, are poised to chart a new course for Indiana’s energy future. Together, we’re working to advance a clean, safe, reliable solution to meet growing energy demand and benefit Indiana and its communities for generations to come,” said J. Clay Sell, CEO of X-energy.

Blackstone Raises $8.7bn at Hard Cap for Energy Transition Fund V
- Fund size: The final close is more than 50 per cent larger than the predecessor fund.
- Investor demand: The fund was significantly oversubscribed and reached its hard cap.
- Early deployment: Three platform companies funded and three acquisitions completed.
Blackstone has announced the final close of Blackstone Energy Transition Partners V (BETP V) at $8.7 billion. Notably, the fund is more than 50 per cent larger than its predecessor. It was significantly oversubscribed and reached its hard cap, the maximum size the fund can reach.
BETP’s strategy focuses on building large-scale energy businesses that support growing global demand for cleaner, more reliable and affordable energy. As of June 30, the strategy had generated a 34 per cent net internal rate of return (IRR) since 1997. Separately, in 2025, IJ Investor named BETP Fund Manager of the Year – Equity for North America. The announcement did not disclose a target fund size, investor names or the closing date.
BETP V began its investment period in June and has already funded three platform companies: Kindle, Fisterra and Viridon. Together, these investments support new power generation capacity and electricity transmission infrastructure. The fund has also completed three acquisitions focused on energy efficiency and infrastructure resilience.
“We believe there is a generational opportunity for experienced investors in the energy transition to provide solutions to the challenges posed by growing demand for electricity. By backing exceptional management teams with flexible, patient equity capital to increase manufacturing capacity, recruit and train skilled labour and construct new critical energy infrastructure assets, BETP is delivering those solutions and in the process building these companies to scale, creating jobs and generating lasting value for our investors. We are deeply grateful for the trust of our investors and look forward to deploying BETP V in investments that advance the transition to a more affordable, reliable and cleaner energy future,” said David Foley, Global Head of Blackstone Energy Transition Partners at Blackstone.

Since January 2025, BETP has committed more than $11 billion in new equity across the energy transition sector. Investments include power equipment makers Maclean Power Systems and Delta Star, and essential services providers Alliance Technical Group and Shermco. Meanwhile, the firm has monetised mature predecessor-fund investments, including an agreement to sell Aypa Power, a 6.0-gigawatt battery storage portfolio. Legence, a provider of engineering and mechanical contracting services, also listed through an initial public offering.

BETP gains a data centre liquid cooling components business through Flow Control Holdings, while DarkVision adds technology-enabled inspection for critical energy infrastructure. It also adds measurement, control and repair products for gas and water utilities through Dresser Utility Solutions. That positions BETP to sell engineered cooling components to data centre customers, provided demand for liquid cooling keeps rising.

articles.title: Inpe Records 42% Drop in Brazil’s Amazon Deforestation, to 3,335 sq km
articles.summary:
Deforestation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest fell to about 3,335 square kilometers in the 12 months through July, the lowest on record. That is a decline of about 42% from the […]
The post Inpe Records 42% Drop in Brazil’s Amazon Deforestation, to 3,335 sq km appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Inpe Records 42% Drop in Brazil’s Amazon Deforestation, to 3,335 sq km
- Record Amazon low: About 3,335 square kilometers were cleared in the 12 months through July, the lowest since records began in 1988.
- Steep annual drop: Clearing fell about 42%, well below the previous low of 4,571 square kilometers set in 2011-2012.
- Cerrado also down: Savanna deforestation fell about 24% to some 5,517 square kilometers, a record low for a series starting in 2001.
Deforestation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest fell to about 3,335 square kilometers in the 12 months through July, the lowest on record. That is a decline of about 42% from the preceding period, according to data released on October 16 by Inpe, Brazil’s space research agency. The historical series goes back to 1988.
In Brazil’s Cerrado savanna, deforestation fell about 24% over the same period, to some 5,517 square kilometers. That was also the lowest level in an Inpe series that starts in 2001. “The figures released today are a historic achievement,” said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima, adding they show the world that “with political will, it is possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions.”
Inpe produces the figures once a year through PRODES, its satellite monitoring program. PRODES measures from August to July, because lighter cloud cover in the middle of the year hides less deforestation on satellite images. The reported figures did not break the decline down by state or identify its main drivers.
RELATED ARTICLE: Amazon Deforestation in Brazil Hits 9-Year Low, Reports Government
Track Record
The previous record low for Brazil’s Amazon was 4,571 square kilometers, reached in 2011-2012. In the mid-1990s, annual destruction peaked at nearly 30,000 square kilometers. Deforestation later soared to its highest level in 15 years under former President Jair Bolsonaro. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva took office in 2023 pledging to end deforestation by 2030.
Who It Affects
- Presidential candidates: Lula faces Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, in a presidential election runoff on October 25, after the senator performed better than expected in the first round.
- Amazon pressure zones: Flavio Bolsonaro’s manifesto pledges stronger environmental oversight in the Amazon, prioritizing areas under the greatest pressure from deforestation and wildfires.
- Extractive workers and small farmers: Flavio Bolsonaro said law enforcement under his plan would focus on organized crime rather than on these groups.
